project_scope.note: This is the initial Fagaceae family file for the current Hays Botany ID build. Future genera should be merged into it, not blindly replace it.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: If fruit is present, find the nut and cupule first. In local Quercus this means an acorn sitting in a scaly cup. Then read mature leaves, buds/twigs, bark and cupule details.
family_diagnostics.leaves: Alternate simple leaves with stipules; local oak species vary strongly in lobing, margins, underside hairs and persistence.
family_diagnostics.flowers: Unisexual; staminate flowers commonly in catkins. Flowers are less useful than fruit/vegetative characters for routine local oak ID.
family_diagnostics.fruit: A nut associated with a cupule; in Quercus the acorn/cup is decisive family confirmation.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Simple leaf + acorn/cupule is the fast family pattern. Use leaf, bud, bark and cupule for species.

look_here_first_sequence.plain: a hard acorn sitting in its scaly cup
look_here_first_sequence.look: Examine a mature attached acorn; follow the cup scales to the nut base.
look_here_first_sequence.why: A true oak acorn cup is not a walnut husk, Prunus fleshy drupe or willow capsule.

look_here_first_sequence.formal: alternate simple leaves and terminal buds
look_here_first_sequence.plain: one leaf per node, and a cluster of scaly buds at a twig tip
look_here_first_sequence.look: Use several mature leaves and twig tips from the SAME tree; inspect upper and lower leaf surfaces.
look_here_first_sequence.why: Separates local Quercus from compound-leaved Juglandaceae and supports species-level routing; leaf shape alone is unreliable.

look_here_first_sequence.formal: bristle-tipped vs rounded lobes; abaxial indumentum
look_here_first_sequence.plain: tiny sharp points on some leaf tips, plus hairs on the leaf underside
look_here_first_sequence.look: Inspect lobe tips and the underside with a hand lens; bristles often suggest red-oak group, but not a universal family rule.
look_here_first_sequence.why: Routes oak groups, then needs buds and cupules to resolve variable leaves.

look_here_first_sequence.look: Confirm with fruit or twig/leaf suite; catkins also occur in walnuts and willows.
look_here_first_sequence.why: Useful supporting clue, not a stand-alone family diagnosis.

family_diagnostics.important_exceptions: This Central Texas lesson routes the canonical Quercus pool, not every Fagaceae genus: chestnuts and beeches also make cupule-associated nuts but not typical single-acorn oak cups. Oak leaves can be entire, toothed or lobed, deciduous or evergreen. Juvenile shoots, shade, drought and hybridization alter leaves; red-oak bristles and bud clusters are aids, not universal or sufficient by themselves.
family_diagnostics.genus_routing: Current canonical Fagaceae representatives are Quercus. First verify the acorn/cupule; for Quercus use mature leaf lobe tips, abaxial hairs, terminal buds, cupule shape/scale texture and habitat together. Compare Q. buckleyi (bristle-tipped red oak), Q. fusiformis (live-oak leaf/catkin context), Q. stellata (rounded lobes and twig traits) and Q. marilandica (broad distal bristle-tipped lobes and tawny buds). Do not imply these four are the only family members.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: attached nut + cupule → leaf tips/underside → bud cluster/twig → male catkins as supporting clue → walnut/Prunus/willow fruit contrasts
visual_lesson.intro: Oaks are easiest when the acorn teaches the family and the leaf/bud/cup teaches the species.

steps.title: 1 · Find the cupule
steps.look_for: A nut seated in a scaly cupule.
steps.why_it_matters: The acorn + cupule combination is the strongest local Fagaceae cue.
steps.photo_warning: Existing Q. fusiformis anchor is not evidence of a visible cupule; use the verified Q. marilandica acorn-and-cup image below for that exact role.

steps.title: 2 · Read the mature leaf
steps.look_for: Simple alternate leaf; note lobes, tips, margin and underside.
steps.why_it_matters: Leaf architecture narrows local oak groups quickly.
steps.photo_warning: External CC BY 4.0 leaf photograph: bristle-tipped lobes and venation visible; no underside hairs, buds or acorns.

steps.title: 3 · Check the twig and bud
steps.look_for: Bud size/shape, clustering and twig pubescence.
steps.why_it_matters: Bud/twig traits remain useful when acorns are absent.
steps.photo_warning: Existing Q. laceyi images have not been confirmed here to show diagnostic bud-scale detail.

steps.title: 4 · Compare bark + leaf + cup
steps.look_for: Use several characters together instead of forcing one leaf shape.
steps.why_it_matters: Oaks hybridize and vary; multi-character ID is safer.
steps.photo_warning: Do not use a single Q. stellata reference photo as proof of leaf, bark AND cupule anatomy.

steps.title: 5 · See the scaly cup on an actual oak nut
steps.photo_role: attached acorn, cupule scales and twig macro
steps.look_for: The hard acorn is held at its base by a separate cup with overlapping scales. Follow the cup rim around the nut; do not mistake the whole walnut husk for an oak cup.
steps.why_it_matters: This photograph supplies the actual cupule view missing from the generic first step. Nut ripeness and dimensions cannot be determined without a scale.

steps.title: 6 · Compare bristle tips and bud hairs
steps.photo_role: separate mature leaf and terminal-bud macro examples
steps.look_for: Tawny hairs on the clustered terminal buds and twig; compare a separate adult leaf photograph for the broad, distal bristle-tipped lobes.
steps.why_it_matters: A real bud macro can resolve an oak when leaves are variable. The bud image alone does not prove the leaf-lobe character.

steps.title: 7 · Inspect a broad bristle-tipped leaf
steps.photo_role: mature upper leaf face and distal bristle-tipped lobes
steps.look_for: Leaf blade broadest toward its tip, with projecting distal lobes; minute bristle tips are small and require magnification.
steps.why_it_matters: Contrast with Q. stellata rounded lobes; do not identify from a single leaf, especially on sprouts or hybrids.

comparisons.title: Fagaceae vs Juglandaceae
comparisons.rule: Local oaks have simple leaves + acorn/cupule. Walnuts have pinnately compound leaves + a husked nut. Both can have catkins.

comparisons.title: Fagaceae vs Rosaceae (Prunus)
comparisons.rule: An oak nut is seated in a distinct scaly cupule. A plum/cherry has a fleshy drupe around a hard endocarp (stone), without an oak cup. Leaves can overlap; inspect attached fruit and twig.

comparisons.title: Fagaceae vs Salicaceae (Salix/Populus)
comparisons.rule: Both can have unisexual catkins and alternate simple leaves. Local Salicaceae releases numerous silky-haired seeds from split dry capsules; Quercus bears a single hard acorn seated in a scaly cupule.

visual_lesson.caveat: Catkins alone do not distinguish oaks from walnuts; use leaf architecture and fruit. This is a Quercus-led local family lesson, not a claim that all Fagaceae have oak-style acorns. A photo is only evidence for structures actually resolved in it; annotations remain pending.
